c.tagline: Oscar Niemeyer's modernist capital, sculpted from the Cerrado plateau.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered; airport and long cross-wing trips can be pricey given the city's huge distances, so ride-hail apps are often cheaper.

emergency.note: 190 reaches the Military Police, 192 the SAMU ambulance service, and 193 the fire brigade (Corpo de Bombeiros).

avoid.reason: Avoid the poorer satellite cities such as Estrutural and parts of Ceilândia after dark, where street crime is markedly higher than in the Plano Piloto.
Watch for phone snatching and pickpockets around the central Rodoviária bus platform, especially at night, and use ride apps rather than walking the empty superquadra stretches late.

hood_desc: The southern half of the residential 'wings', built from Lúcio Costa's numbered superblocks (superquadras); it holds the Hotel Sector, the liveliest concentration of restaurants and bars (around blocks 405/406 and the Setor de Clubes), and is the most convenient base for first-time visitors.

The northern residential wing, mirror image of Asa Sul, anchored by the University of Brasília and Parque da Cidade; leafier and a touch calmer, with growing dining pockets and a younger, more local feel.

An upscale lakeside district of low-rise mansions, embassies, and the Pontão do Lago Sul waterfront with restaurants and marinas; green, quiet, and affluent, best for travelers wanting calm and views over Paranoá Lake.

The ceremonial core along the Monumental Axis and the adjacent Hotel Sector (Setor Hoteleiro), home to Niemeyer's National Congress, the Cathedral, the Three Powers Square, and most of the city's headline monuments and museums; where sightseers stay to be steps from the landmarks.

A dense, fast-growing residential satellite southwest of the Plano Piloto, well served by the metro and full of high-rise apartments, shopping, and everyday amenities; a practical, affordable base for longer stays.

water.note: Treated and generally safe in the Plano Piloto, though most locals drink it filtered.

transit.hours: The Metrô-DF runs from about 06:00 to 23:30 Monday to Saturday and 07:00 to 19:00 on Sundays; buses cover longer hours, with limited late-night service on key corridors.
transit.note: The two-line Metrô-DF mainly links the western satellite cities to the central bus station and is of limited use inside the Plano Piloto itself, where DFTrans buses and ride-hail apps are the practical way to get around this very spread-out, car-oriented city.
transit.pay: Load a rechargeable Bilhete Único do DF card or tap a contactless card at metro gates and on most buses. A single metro or bus ride costs about R$5.50 (roughly $1), with discounted transfers between bus and metro within a set window.

bus: Rodoviária do Plano Piloto (central bus station)

transit.m: Expresso Aeroporto / bus line 0.113 to the Plano Piloto central bus station ~40 min
Taxi to the Hotel Sector / Plano Piloto ~20 min
Uber or 99 ride-hail to the city center ~15-20 min

tip.r: A 10% service charge is usually added to restaurant bills; extra tipping is optional.

food.desc: Brasilia's daily ritual: load a plate from a huge buffet of rice, beans, grilled meats and salads and pay by the weight.

places.name: Mangai

places.name: Naturetto

places.name: Feira Central de Ceilândia food boxes

places.name: Feira Central de Ceilândia

places.name: Mangai

places.name: Feira da Torre de TV

places.name: Feira Central de Ceilândia

places.name: Bar Beirute

places.name: Feira Permanente do Núcleo Bandeirante

places.name: Feira da Torre de TV
places.note: Weekend stalls carry empadão and other Central-West savoury bakes.

places.name: Bar Beirute
places.note: The classic Brasilia bar crowd, open-air tables and long cachaça and beer list.

places.name: Bar do Calaf

places.name: Feitiço Mineiro

landmarks: Catedral Metropolitana de Brasília
Oscar Niemeyer's crown-shaped, hyperboloid cathedral with soaring stained-glass panels is the singular architectural symbol of Brazil's capital.
Congresso Nacional (National Congress)
The iconic twin towers flanked by a bowl-shaped dome and inverted dome define Brasília's skyline and are instantly recognizable as the seat of Brazil's legislature.
Palácio do Planalto
The sleek, colonnaded presidential workplace exemplifies Niemeyer's modernist vision and is a centerpiece of the Praça dos Três Poderes.
Palácio da Alvorada
The official presidential residence, famous for its slender, elegant white columns that appear to float above a reflecting pool.
Memorial JK
A striking monument honoring Juscelino Kubitschek, the president who founded Brasília, topped by a distinctive statue and star-shaped design.
Torre de TV (TV Tower)
A 224-meter lattice tower with an observation deck offering sweeping views of the city's unique airplane-shaped urban plan.
Praça dos Três Poderes
The vast ceremonial plaza where Brazil's executive, legislative, and judicial powers converge, ringed by some of the city's most photographed modernist landmarks.
Teatro Nacional Cláudio Santoro
A monumental pyramid-shaped concrete theater that stands as one of the boldest examples of Niemeyer's civic architecture.
Santuário Dom Bosco
A luminous blue-glass church whose thousands of stained-glass panels bathe the interior in an otherworldly blue light at night.
Ponte JK (JK Bridge)
An award-winning bridge over Lake Paranoá with three asymmetrically crossing steel arches, a striking feat of modern engineering especially at sunset.

train.note: No intercity passenger rail. Brasília has a two-line metro serving the satellite towns, but Brazil runs no long-distance passenger trains from the capital. Travel is by coach or plane.

bus.note: No international coaches. The Rodoviária Interestadual (not the central Rodoviária do Plano Piloto, which is city buses only) is west of the centre and handles the long-distance network - São Paulo about 14 hours, Belo Horizonte 10, Goiânia 3. Book through ClickBus (https://www.clickbus.com.br/) or Buser (https://www.buser.com.br/); flying is far quicker for the long routes.

ferry.note: Brasília is a planned city on the central plateau with no navigable water beyond the artificial Lake Paranoá, which carries pleasure boats but no scheduled service, so there are no ferries.

half.name: Pirenópolis
half.blurb: Colonial-era gold-mining town of cobblestone streets, waterfalls and swimming holes in the hills of Goiás state.

half.name: Cristalina
half.blurb: Plateau town known for its quartz-crystal shops and rolling cerrado scenery, a straightforward drive south of the capital.

full.name: Chapada dos Veadeiros
full.blurb: High-altitude national park of dramatic canyons and waterfalls in the Cerrado, a UNESCO World Heritage site.
